notes.meaning: The writer cries out to the Lord because he is trapped in a tight spot of deep distress. He looks back on how God answered his prayers in the past, and this gives him fresh confidence for today. When troubles press in from every side, calling on God is always our best refuge.

The writer begs God to save his life from dishonest people who spread wicked gossip and lies about him. False words can cut down an innocent person's good name like a weapon, and human effort alone cannot stop them. He turns to the Lord because only God has the power to restrain evil tongues and guard the truth.

The writer turns to address the slanderer directly, asking what kind of payback such a deceitful tongue expects to receive. A person who ruins others with lies gains nothing good for their soul in the end. God sees every false word, and the liar will surely have to answer to Him.

The judgment awaiting the liar is described as sharp arrows from a powerful warrior and burning coals of the desert broom tree. Coals from this bush burn with an intense heat and stay hot for a very long time. Just as the slanderer's words pierced and burned others, God will answer them with sharp and lasting justice.

The writer grieves that he feels like an exile living among brutal, warlike people, comparing them to the distant lands of Meshech and Kedar. He did not actually travel to those nations; rather, his dishonest neighbors acted just as cruel and lawless as those foreign tribes. It is deeply painful for someone who loves God to be stuck among people who mock the truth.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: In the traditional Latin Vulgate and Douay-Rheims translation, the first part is read as a lament that the speaker's exile has been prolonged, rather than naming Meshech directly.

notes.meaning: The writer complains that he has spent far too long living alongside people who despise peace. These neighbors love strife and make daily life exhausting for anyone trying to live right. Believers often feel like strangers when surrounded by an ungodly culture that thrives on conflict.

The writer is devoted to peace in his heart, but whenever he speaks to seek reconciliation, his enemies demand war. His kind and reasonable words are rejected by people whose hearts are bent on doing harm. Even when our attempts to make peace are turned away, God calls us to keep pursuing love and calm.
